# Learning Atlas research pack

This is a generated exploration surface for NotebookLM or another source-grounded reading tool. The repository is authoritative. Follow source URLs for the original work; this pack contains original synthesis, not copyrighted papers.

## How to interrogate this pack

Ask for the evidence chain behind a principle, disagreements between sources, boundary conditions, missing evidence, and experiments that could change a belief. Do not treat generated answers as new atlas evidence.

## S001 — Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning outcomes

Type: source  
Status: reviewed  
Topics: learning-vs-performance, ai-tutoring, scaffolding, assessment-validity  
Canonical path: `sources/notes/S001-bastani-generative-ai-guardrails.md`

# S001 — Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning outcomes

## Why it matters

This study directly separates performance while AI is available from later performance after access is removed. It is unusually relevant to the risk that an AI learning product optimizes visible completion while eroding independent capability.

## Study

A preregistered field experiment involved nearly 1,000 students in high-school mathematics classes. Students received access to either a general-purpose GPT interface, a tutor with pedagogical guardrails, or no AI during practice. A later exam removed AI access.

## Findings

Both AI conditions improved supported practice performance. Students who had used the unrestricted interface subsequently performed worse without it than the control group. The safeguarded tutor substantially reduced this negative learning effect. The result supports neither “AI harms learning” nor “AI tutors work” in general; it shows that interaction design can change the relationship between assisted performance and independent performance.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

The work covers a particular mathematics curriculum, age group, implementation, and relatively short horizon. Treatment contrast combines several interface and pedagogical differences. It does not establish long-term retention, far transfer, or broad generality across subjects and learners.

## Evidence profile

| Dimension | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Internal validity | high | Preregistered randomized field design with a no-AI comparison |
| Directness | high | Directly compares AI-assisted practice with independent assessment |
| Consistency | moderate | Direction aligns with the broader learning/performance distinction; exact intervention needs replication |
| Replication | low | The specific treatment contrast is not yet independently replicated here |
| Magnitude | moderate | Practically meaningful differences were reported |
| Duration | low | Follow-up is short |
| Transfer | low | Assessment remains close to the taught mathematics |
| Ecological validity | high | Conducted in authentic classrooms |

## Candidate claims

Supports [C001] and [C002]. It is central evidence for progressive assistance [P001] and independent outcome measurement [P005].

# S002 — AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning

## Why it matters

It tests a deliberately structured AI tutor in an authentic university course rather than treating an unprompted chatbot as the intervention.

## Study and findings

In a randomized controlled trial with 194 students in an undergraduate physics course, a carefully designed AI tutoring lesson was compared with in-class active learning. Students in the AI condition learned more in less time and reported greater engagement and motivation. The tutor used research-based constraints and detailed instructional design.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

This was a single course, institution, set of lessons, and implementation. Outcomes were short-term and close to instruction. The study compares a particular tutor lesson with a particular active-learning lesson, not AI with all human teaching. The authors explicitly caution against universal extrapolation.

## Evidence profile

| Dimension | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Internal validity | high | Randomized comparison in an authentic course |
| Directness | high | Tests a structured AI tutor and learning outcomes |
| Consistency | moderate | Compatible with tutoring research and other structured AI interventions |
| Replication | low | The particular design requires independent replication |
| Magnitude | moderate | Reported learning and efficiency gains were substantial |
| Duration | low | Short-term outcomes |
| Transfer | low | No strong evidence of far transfer |
| Ecological validity | moderate | Real course, but a tightly designed intervention |

## Candidate claims

Supports [C002] while making the design of the pedagogical harness a necessary boundary condition.

# S003 — Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance

## Why it matters

This preprint provides a design vocabulary for learning-first AI companions across pedagogical, adaptive, and responsible foundations. It closely matches the atlas distinction between output assistance and capability development.

## Argument

The framework argues that educational companions should diagnose and adapt, preserve learner agency, use evidence-based pedagogy, and optimize learning rather than task completion. It connects design decisions across interaction, learner modelling, and responsibility rather than presenting a single tutoring technique.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

This is a recent preprint and framework, not itself causal evidence that the full framework improves learning. Its components need empirical testing, operational definitions, and comparison with alternative architectures.

## Evidence profile

| Dimension | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Internal validity | not-applicable | Design framework rather than intervention study |
| Directness | high | Directly addresses learning-first AI companion design |
| Consistency | moderate | Integrates established learning-science constructs |
| Replication | not-applicable | Framework components require evaluation |
| Magnitude | not-applicable | No pooled intervention effect |
| Duration | unclear | Longitudinal implications are proposed rather than established |
| Transfer | unclear | Requires testing |
| Ecological validity | moderate | Designed for realistic systems but not proof of deployment effectiveness |

## Candidate claims

Useful design synthesis for [B001], [B003], and [P001], but should not be treated as primary outcome evidence.

# S004 — OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026

## Why it matters

The report synthesizes emerging evidence and policy questions about effective generative-AI use in education. It foregrounds a recurring pattern: general-purpose AI may improve the quality of immediate work without producing equivalent learning.

## Synthesis

The OECD distinguishes generic task assistance from tools and practices designed with pedagogical intent. It discusses roles for teachers, institutions, evaluation, and governance, and emphasizes that educational value depends on use and design rather than access alone.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

This is a broad institutional synthesis, not one homogeneous systematic review or causal study. The evidence base is fast moving, and examples vary in maturity, populations, outcomes, and methods. Follow primary citations before using a specific reported effect.

## Evidence profile

| Dimension | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Internal validity | not-applicable | Multi-source policy synthesis |
| Directness | high | Directly concerns GenAI and educational outcomes |
| Consistency | moderate | Identifies convergent patterns while acknowledging mixed evidence |
| Replication | unclear | Depends on the underlying study |
| Magnitude | unclear | Not represented by one effect |
| Duration | moderate | Explicitly raises durable learning, but evidence remains limited |
| Transfer | moderate | Covers diverse systems without proving cross-context transfer |
| Ecological validity | high | Institutional and implementation constraints are central |

## Candidate claims

Supports the framing of [C001] and the need for [P005]. Use underlying primary studies for narrower causal claims.

# S005 — From Chalkboards to Chatbots

## Why it matters

This study broadens the evidence beyond affluent universities and tests a structured, teacher-supported GenAI programme in a low-resource secondary-school setting.

## Study and findings

A six-week after-school programme in Nigeria combined Microsoft Copilot/GPT-4 access with teacher facilitation and a structured curriculum. The randomized evaluation reports a 0.31 standard-deviation gain on a combined outcome and a 0.23 standard-deviation gain in English. The World Bank publishes a reproducibility package for the analysis.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

The intervention is a bundle: technology, teacher support, structured sessions, additional time, and curriculum. Results do not identify the independent contribution of the model or generalize automatically to unsupervised use, other ages, or longer-term outcomes. Retention and transfer beyond the study measures require more evidence.

## Evidence profile

| Dimension | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Internal validity | high | Randomized evaluation with public reproducibility materials |
| Directness | moderate | Relevant to structured AI learning, but the bundled intervention differs from a standalone product |
| Consistency | moderate | Compatible with structured-tutor evidence |
| Replication | low | Context-specific programme not independently replicated here |
| Magnitude | moderate | Reported effects are educationally meaningful |
| Duration | low | Six-week programme with limited delayed evidence |
| Transfer | low | Outcomes do not establish broad transfer |
| Ecological validity | high | Real low-resource school setting and facilitation constraints |

## Candidate claims

Supports [C002] with teacher mediation and structure as essential boundary conditions.

## S006 — Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention

# S006 — Test-Enhanced Learning

## Why it matters

The experiments demonstrate the classic divergence between conditions that look best immediately and those that produce better delayed retention.

## Study and findings

Students studied prose passages and then either restudied or practised retrieval. Restudy could benefit very short-delay performance, while prior retrieval produced stronger retention after longer delays. Retrieval is therefore both an assessment event and a learning event under appropriate conditions.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

Laboratory prose learning is narrower than authentic capability. Retrieval quality, corrective feedback, knowledge type, test format, and delay matter. Retrieval practice is not a warrant for constant high-stakes testing.

## Evidence profile

| Dimension | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Internal validity | high | Controlled experiments with clear treatment contrasts |
| Directness | high | Directly compares restudy and retrieval over time |
| Consistency | high | Supported by a large subsequent literature |
| Replication | high | Retrieval effects are widely replicated |
| Magnitude | moderate | Effects are robust but moderator-dependent |
| Duration | moderate | Includes delayed tests, though not long-term field outcomes |
| Transfer | low | Original experiments focus retention more than broad transfer |
| Ecological validity | low | Laboratory tasks and passages |

## Candidate claims

Supports [C004], [P004], and the outcome hierarchy in the epistemic policy.

# S007 — Transfer of Test-Enhanced Learning

## Why it matters

It tests whether retrieval benefits survive changes between practice and final assessment rather than merely reproducing the same item.

## Review and findings

The meta-analysis synthesized 192 effect sizes from 122 experiments involving 10,382 participants. Retrieval practice improved transfer overall (reported mean effect approximately `d = 0.40`), with important moderators related to the degree and kind of transfer, retrieval format, feedback, and materials.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

“Transfer” spans materially different distances. A positive mean does not guarantee far transfer, workplace performance, or benefit for every retrieval design. Publication bias and dependence among effects require attention in interpreting any pooled estimate.

## Evidence profile

| Dimension | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Internal validity | moderate | Synthesizes mostly controlled experiments with varying quality |
| Directness | high | Transfer from retrieval practice is the target question |
| Consistency | moderate | Positive overall with meaningful moderators |
| Replication | high | Large set of experiments |
| Magnitude | moderate | Mean effect is meaningful, not universal |
| Duration | moderate | Delays vary across studies |
| Transfer | high | Explicitly examines changed final-test contexts |
| Ecological validity | low | Much evidence remains laboratory based |

## Candidate claims

Supports [C004] while constraining claims about far or authentic transfer.

# S008 — Distributed Practice in Verbal Recall Tasks

## Why it matters

Spacing is foundational for a learning engine that can choose not only what comes next but when to revisit it.

## Review and findings

The quantitative synthesis covers 317 experiments reported in 184 articles. Distributed practice generally improves later verbal recall relative to massed practice. The effective gap between study events depends on the desired retention interval; there is no context-free optimal spacing schedule.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

The review concentrates on verbal recall. The relationship between spacing and complex skill acquisition, collaborative practice, motivation, and authentic workplace performance needs more targeted evidence. Product scheduling must account for dropout and opportunity costs.

## Evidence profile

| Dimension | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Internal validity | moderate | Large synthesis of heterogeneous experiments |
| Directness | high | Directly evaluates distributed versus massed practice for recall |
| Consistency | high | Broadly consistent benefit with quantitative moderators |
| Replication | high | Hundreds of experiments |
| Magnitude | moderate | Depends strongly on intervals and task conditions |
| Duration | high | Retention interval is central to the analysis |
| Transfer | low | Primarily verbal recall rather than transfer |
| Ecological validity | low | Many studies use controlled memory tasks |

## Candidate claims

Supports [C005] and [P004].

# S009 — The Expertise Reversal Effect

## Why it matters

Personalization cannot mean “more guidance for everyone.” Support that reduces extraneous load for a novice may become redundant, inefficient, or harmful as expertise grows.

## Review and argument

The paper synthesizes evidence that the effectiveness of instructional techniques interacts with learner expertise. Detailed guidance, worked information, and explanatory support can help novices but impose redundant processing on more knowledgeable learners.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

Expertise is domain-specific and difficult to infer reliably. The effect does not imply abandoning all support for experts or linearly reducing help. Task novelty, element interactivity, goals, and assessment quality matter.

## Evidence profile

| Dimension | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Internal validity | moderate | Theoretical synthesis grounded in multiple experiments |
| Directness | high | Directly concerns expertise-contingent guidance |
| Consistency | moderate | Repeated pattern with contextual variation |
| Replication | moderate | Observed across multiple instructional techniques |
| Magnitude | unclear | No single pooled magnitude |
| Duration | unclear | Often measured over relatively short learning episodes |
| Transfer | unclear | Varies by cited study |
| Ecological validity | moderate | Design principle is plausible, but reliable deployment needs learner-state evidence |

## Candidate claims

Supports [C003], [B005], and [P003].

# S010 — The Power of Feedback

## Why it matters

Generative systems can produce unlimited feedback; the educational challenge is selecting feedback that changes the learner’s next action without replacing the thinking.

## Synthesis

The review organizes feedback around the questions “Where am I going?”, “How am I going?”, and “Where to next?”, and distinguishes feedback about task, process, self-regulation, and self. Feedback effects vary substantially and can be positive or negative depending on focus, timing, interpretation, and context.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

The synthesis predates generative AI and covers heterogeneous studies. Its taxonomy is a useful design lens, not a guarantee that every process-level prompt improves learning. Feedback uptake and learner trust must be measured.

## Evidence profile

| Dimension | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Internal validity | moderate | Broad review of heterogeneous evidence |
| Directness | high | Directly concerns feedback design and learning |
| Consistency | moderate | Effects differ meaningfully by feedback type |
| Replication | high | Draws on a large evidence base |
| Magnitude | unclear | Large heterogeneity makes one magnitude misleading |
| Duration | unclear | Varies across studies |
| Transfer | unclear | Varies across feedback targets and studies |
| Ecological validity | high | Framework spans authentic teaching contexts |

## Candidate claims

Supports [C006] and constrains simplistic “more feedback” product strategies.

## S011 — Knowledge Tracing: Modeling the Acquisition of Procedural Knowledge

# S011 — Knowledge Tracing

## Why it matters

Knowledge tracing is an early influential account of updating estimates of skill mastery from learner opportunities and responses. It offers both a useful architecture and a warning: a learner model is an inference under assumptions, not a transcript of the mind.

## Model

The work models acquisition of procedural knowledge over successive practice opportunities using latent mastery and probabilities for learning, guessing, and slipping. These estimates can support adaptive problem selection and tutoring decisions.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

Model quality depends on skill decomposition, observation quality, stationarity assumptions, and fit between logged responses and the target construct. Correctness can reflect guessing, assistance, collaboration, or flawed items. Modern models may predict better while remaining difficult to interpret or validate as capability measures.

## Evidence profile

| Dimension | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Internal validity | moderate | Formal model with empirical evaluation, but strong assumptions |
| Directness | high | Directly concerns learner-state inference |
| Consistency | high | Established a large continuing research programme |
| Replication | high | Knowledge-tracing families are widely studied |
| Magnitude | not-applicable | Predictive performance varies by model and data |
| Duration | moderate | Sequential learning is represented, not necessarily long-term retention |
| Transfer | low | Skill estimates are typically local to modelled tasks |
| Ecological validity | moderate | Deployed in tutoring systems but sensitive to instrumentation |

## Candidate claims

Contributes to [C007], [B003], and [P002].

# S012 — Enacting Assessment Reform in a Time of Artificial Intelligence

## Why it matters

The guidance treats assessment reform as a system-design problem under ubiquitous AI, not merely a detection problem. It is directly relevant to trustworthy capability judgments in higher education.

## Argument

The report advocates programme-level assessment design using multiple, inclusive, and contextualized approaches. Trustworthy judgments should draw on accumulated evidence and purposeful opportunities for students to demonstrate capability under different conditions, including appropriate AI use.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

This is expert and sector guidance rather than a causal trial of one assessment architecture. Institutions differ in discipline, regulation, resources, and risk. The recommendations require operational validation and careful treatment of equity and accessibility.

# S013 — Validity of Psychological Assessment

## Why it matters

It redirects attention from whether a score is “valid” in isolation to whether the interpretation and use of evidence are justified, including their consequences.

## Argument

Messick presents validity as an integrated evaluative judgment about the adequacy and appropriateness of interpretations and actions based on assessment evidence. Construct representation, irrelevant variance, value implications, and consequences all matter.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

This is foundational theory, not a recipe for validating an AI learner model. Later standards and debates refine the framework. Specific system claims still require an explicit validation argument and empirical evidence.

## Evidence profile

| Dimension | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Internal validity | not-applicable | Conceptual validity framework |
| Directness | high | Directly governs interpretations from learner evidence |
| Consistency | high | Foundational to modern assessment validity discourse |
| Replication | not-applicable | Not an intervention effect |
| Magnitude | not-applicable | Not an intervention effect |
| Duration | high | Addresses general inference and use over time |
| Transfer | high | Framework applies across assessment contexts |
| Ecological validity | high | Consequences and use are integral to the framework |

## Candidate claims

Supports [C007], [C008], [P002], and [P006].

# S014 — Relative effectiveness of tutoring systems

## Why it matters

The review challenges the simplistic idea that human tutoring is an indivisible gold standard and asks which interaction granularity and feedback mechanisms account for tutoring effects.

## Review and findings

VanLehn compares effect sizes across human tutoring, intelligent tutoring systems, and other tutoring arrangements. Step-based intelligent tutoring systems can approach the effectiveness of human tutoring in the studied domains, suggesting that timely, task-linked interaction matters.

## Limitations and boundary conditions

The review predates large language models and draws heavily from structured STEM problem-solving systems. Effect estimates depend on comparison conditions, outcome alignment, study quality, and domain. Conversational fluency should not be assumed equivalent to step-level pedagogical effectiveness.

## Evidence profile

| Dimension | Rating | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Internal validity | moderate | Review aggregates heterogeneous comparisons |
| Directness | moderate | Relevant to AI tutoring architecture, but predates GenAI |
| Consistency | moderate | Effects vary by tutor and comparison type |
| Replication | high | Draws on many tutoring evaluations |
| Magnitude | moderate | Meaningful effects, conditional on design and comparator |
| Duration | unclear | Many studies emphasize post-tests |
| Transfer | unclear | Domain and outcome dependent |
| Ecological validity | moderate | Includes deployed systems but often structured domains |

## Candidate claims

Provides historical support for [C002] and for designing interaction around learning processes rather than conversational realism.

## C001 — Assisted performance is not evidence of durable learning

Type: claim  
Status: provisional  
Topics: learning-vs-performance, assessment-validity, ai-tutoring  
Canonical path: `claims/C001-assisted-performance-is-not-learning.md`

# C001 — Assisted performance is not evidence of durable learning

## Claim

Improved task performance while generative AI is available does not by itself establish independent, durable, or transferable learning. In at least one authentic randomized study, strong assisted gains coexisted with worse later unaided performance [S001].

## Evidence and reasoning

The immediate/delayed divergence is not unique to AI: restudy can look effective at a short interval while retrieval produces better delayed retention [S006]. The OECD synthesis identifies the same distinction as central to responsible educational GenAI use [S004].

## Boundary conditions

This is not the claim that assistance necessarily harms learning. Structured tutoring can improve measured learning [S002, S005]. Effects depend on the interaction, learner, task, duration, and what is measured after support is removed.

## Counterevidence and uncertainty

Longitudinal, independent, and transfer outcomes remain sparse for modern generative systems. Beneficial AI conditions may create capabilities that conventional post-tests under-measure. Those possibilities strengthen the need for better measurement rather than allowing assisted output to stand in for learning.

## Product relevance

Every important learning metric should state assistance state, delay, and transfer distance. A performance-support mode may legitimately optimize immediate outcomes, but it must not silently update an independent-capability estimate from AI-mediated work.

## C002 — Pedagogical structure changes AI learning outcomes

Type: claim  
Status: provisional  
Topics: ai-tutoring, scaffolding, teacher-practice, learning-vs-performance  
Canonical path: `claims/C002-pedagogical-structure-changes-ai-learning-outcomes.md`

# C002 — Pedagogical structure changes AI learning outcomes

## Claim

The educational effect of generative AI depends materially on the surrounding pedagogical design. Structured, research-based tutor interactions and teacher-supported programmes have produced positive learning outcomes [S002, S005], while an unrestricted interface created a performance/learning gap that guardrails reduced [S001].

## Evidence and reasoning

The convergent pattern is promising across secondary mathematics, university physics, and an after-school programme in Nigeria. Earlier intelligent-tutoring research also suggests that step-linked feedback and task structure—not the mere appearance of conversation—can produce meaningful effects [S014].

## Boundary conditions

Each intervention bundles multiple components. We cannot yet infer one universal “AI tutor recipe,” the independent contribution of the model, or durable far transfer. Domain structure, instructor role, dosage, and learner characteristics vary.

## Counterevidence and uncertainty

Novelty, extra time, unusually intensive author-led design, and aligned assessments may inflate results. Independent replications and component studies are priorities.

## Product relevance

Learning products should expose and test their pedagogical policy: when to ask, hint, explain, model, retrieve, delay, and hand control back. Model capability alone is not a learning architecture.

## C003 — Effective guidance varies with learner expertise

Type: claim  
Status: provisional  
Topics: scaffolding, learner-modelling, ai-tutoring  
Canonical path: `claims/C003-guidance-should-vary-with-expertise.md`

# C003 — Effective guidance varies with learner expertise

## Evidence and reasoning

The expertise-reversal literature documents interactions in which guidance that helps novices becomes redundant or harmful for experienced learners [S009]. This makes adaptive support a learning requirement, not merely a preference feature.

## Boundary conditions and uncertainty

Expertise cannot be safely inferred from confidence, job title, or a few correct responses. Different knowledge components within one learner may need different support. Motivation and task novelty can also alter the right degree of guidance.

## Product relevance

Represent support decisions as hypotheses tied to learner evidence. Fade support gradually, preserve an override, and test whether independent outcomes improve.

## C004 — Retrieval practice supports delayed retention and some transfer

Type: claim  
Status: established  
Topics: retrieval-and-spacing, transfer, learning-vs-performance  
Canonical path: `claims/C004-retrieval-supports-retention-and-transfer.md`

# C004 — Retrieval practice supports delayed retention and some transfer

## Evidence and reasoning

Controlled experiments show that retrieval can outperform restudy on delayed tests even when restudy looks better immediately [S006]. A meta-analysis across 192 effects reports positive transfer overall with meaningful moderators [S007].

## Boundary conditions

Near transfer is better supported than far transfer. Retrieval should be appropriately difficult, psychologically safe, and followed by useful feedback when errors would otherwise persist.

## Product relevance

Ask the learner to recall, explain, predict, or produce before revealing an answer. Schedule later independent checks and distinguish retrieval for learning from surveillance or grading.

## C005 — Spacing improves long-term retention

Type: claim

# C005 — Spacing improves long-term retention

## Evidence and reasoning

A synthesis of 317 experiments finds a broad benefit from distributed over massed practice and shows that the useful inter-study gap changes with the target retention interval [S008].

## Boundary conditions

Recall findings do not automatically establish complex-skill transfer. Real systems must balance theoretical schedules with availability, motivation, urgency, and the costs of returning.

## Product relevance

Maintain an evidence-aware revisit queue. Choose spacing against the time horizon at which capability is meant to remain available, and measure whether learners actually return.

## C006 — Feedback is not uniformly beneficial

Type: claim  
Status: provisional  
Topics: feedback, metacognition, motivation-and-agency  
Canonical path: `claims/C006-feedback-effects-depend-on-form-and-context.md`

# C006 — Feedback is not uniformly beneficial

## Evidence and reasoning

Feedback can be powerful, but its effects range from positive to negative. Task, process, and self-regulation information serve different functions, while praise or person-level evaluation can divert attention from the work [S010].

## Boundary conditions and uncertainty

Generative feedback has new properties: abundance, conversational revision, plausible errors, and uncertain learner trust. These require direct contemporary studies rather than simple transfer of older averages.

## Product relevance

Treat feedback as a policy decision. Diagnose before responding, link feedback to goals and next action, create an opportunity to use it, and observe whether the learner revises productively.

## C007 — Learner models are probabilistic inferences, not ground truth

Type: claim  
Status: provisional  
Topics: learner-modelling, assessment-validity, ethics-and-governance  
Canonical path: `claims/C007-learner-models-are-probabilistic-inferences.md`

# C007 — Learner models are probabilistic inferences, not ground truth

## Evidence and reasoning

Knowledge tracing infers latent mastery through assumptions about skills, learning, guesses, slips, and observation sequences [S011]. Validity attaches to the interpretation and use of evidence, not to a score in isolation [S013]. Therefore a learner model cannot responsibly be represented as a context-free fact about a person.

## Boundary conditions

This does not make learner modelling futile. It makes transparency, calibration, validity evidence, and decision-appropriate confidence necessary. Low-stakes content sequencing and high-stakes capability certification demand different assurance.

## Product relevance

Use an evidence ledger: observation, context, assistance state, time, model version, inference, uncertainty, and permitted uses. Let later evidence revise rather than merely accumulate on top of earlier estimates.

# C008 — Trustworthy capability judgments need multiple evidence channels

## Evidence and reasoning

AI makes a submitted artifact a weaker proxy for unaided capability. Sector guidance advocates programme-level, varied, contextualized evidence [S012], while validity theory requires justification of the interpretations and actions drawn from that evidence [S013].

## Boundary conditions

Triangulation is not a vote count. Evidence channels must represent the construct, avoid irrelevant variance, and be sufficiently independent. More surveillance can increase harm without increasing validity.

## Product relevance

Represent what the person did, with what support, under which conditions, and for what intended inference. Allow a portfolio to support a judgment; never let a model-generated label silently become the judgment.

## B001 — Optimize durable capability, not completion

Type: belief  
Status: adopted  
Topics: learning-vs-performance, product-measurement, ai-tutoring  
Canonical path: `beliefs/B001-optimize-capability-not-completion.md`

# B001 — Optimize durable capability, not completion

## Position

The learning engine earns its name only when its objective function extends beyond producing a good artifact today. It should help a person become more capable tomorrow and reveal when it is operating as performance support instead.

## Why we believe this

Assisted performance can diverge from unaided learning [C001]. Structured pedagogy can improve outcomes [C002], and retrieval and spacing show why slower or harder-looking experiences may create more durable memory [C004, C005].

## Strongest counterarguments

People often need to perform now, and AI-mediated collaboration is itself an authentic future capability. The answer is not to reject assistance; it is to distinguish modes and measure the capability each mode claims to develop.

## What would change our mind

We would narrow this belief if reliable longitudinal evidence showed that immediate AI-assisted success was sufficient for the consequential decisions a product makes, or if independent measurement created greater harm than value in a particular setting.

## Implications

The product should declare learning, assessment, and performance-support modes; maintain separate outcomes; and privilege delayed independent and transfer evidence when making a learning claim.

## Revision history

- 2026-08-31: adopted as a founding belief.

## B002 — Preserve productive effort while removing incidental friction

Type: belief  
Status: adopted  
Topics: scaffolding, learning-vs-performance, motivation-and-agency  
Canonical path: `beliefs/B002-preserve-productive-effort.md`

# B002 — Preserve productive effort while removing incidental friction

## Position

Effort is neither automatically virtuous nor automatically waste. The design task is to protect the thinking that changes the learner while removing administrative, accessibility, and interface burdens that do not belong to the target capability.

## Why we believe this

Answer provision can substitute for learning [C001]; retrieval creates learning precisely by requiring generation [C004]; and the useful amount of guidance varies with expertise [C003]. Structured AI can improve learning when it supports rather than bypasses the process [C002].

## Strongest counterarguments

The system cannot observe cognition directly, and its attempt to create “desirable difficulty” can become paternalistic or inaccessible. Learner goals and time pressure matter.

## What would change our mind

We would revise a particular friction judgment when independent outcomes fail to improve, learners cannot access the task equitably, or the effort is unrelated to the declared construct.

## Implications

Use attempt-before-answer, progressive hints, worked-example fading, retrieval, and reflection conditionally. Offer explicit performance support rather than pretending all friction serves learning.

## Revision history

- 2026-08-31: adopted as a founding belief.

## B003 — The evidence-backed learner model is the core compounding asset

Type: belief  
Status: adopted  
Topics: learner-modelling, product-measurement, ai-tutoring  
Canonical path: `beliefs/B003-learner-model-is-core-value.md`

# B003 — The evidence-backed learner model is the core compounding asset

## Position

Content becomes abundant; trustworthy knowledge about what a person can do, how that estimate was formed, and what experience may help next remains scarce. That evidence can compound across interactions if it remains interpretable and revisable.

## Why we believe this

Adaptive guidance requires domain-specific learner evidence [C003]. Learner models are probabilistic, validity-laden inferences [C007], and consequential judgments need multiple evidence channels [C008]. Pedagogical design, not raw model fluency, changes outcomes [C002].

## Strongest counterarguments

Personalization is frequently overclaimed. An opaque model may create false authority, privacy risk, and brittle paths. Strong default sequences may beat complex adaptation.

## What would change our mind

We would demote the learner model from the product core if pre-registered comparisons showed no meaningful learning or decision advantage over transparent non-adaptive designs.

## Implications

Invest in evidence provenance, uncertainty, calibration, construct maps, temporal decay, and user contestability before sophisticated recommendation algorithms.

## Revision history

- 2026-08-31: adopted as a founding belief.

## B004 — Represent independent and AI-assisted capability separately

Type: belief  
Status: adopted  
Topics: assessment-validity, human-ai-collaboration, learner-modelling  
Canonical path: `beliefs/B004-separate-independent-and-assisted-capability.md`

# B004 — Represent independent and AI-assisted capability separately

## Position

Independent capability and effective human-AI collaboration are both valuable and neither should erase the other. A single score cannot responsibly answer both questions.

## Why we believe this

AI-assisted performance may diverge from later independent performance [C001]. Any estimate is an inference tied to its observation context [C007], and trustworthy assessment needs multiple contextualized channels [C008].

## Strongest counterarguments

Work is increasingly sociotechnical, making “independent” performance artificial. Yet decomposition remains useful when a learner must verify output, act during outages, meet regulated requirements, or build foundational understanding.

## What would change our mind

We would replace this separation with a richer model if it preserved the same interpretive clarity while representing teams, tools, autonomy, verification, and changing assistance more faithfully.

## Implications

Tag every observation with assistance conditions. Model AI collaboration capabilities—prompting, verification, judgment, escalation—alongside the target domain capability.

## Revision history

- 2026-08-31: adopted as a founding belief.

## B005 — Personalization must earn its complexity

Type: belief  
Status: adopted  
Topics: learner-modelling, product-measurement, scaffolding  
Canonical path: `beliefs/B005-personalization-must-earn-complexity.md`

# B005 — Personalization must earn its complexity

## Position

Personalization is a causal claim: because the system knows something about this learner, a different action will help. It should be evaluated against simple policies, not assumed valuable because the output feels tailored.

## Why we believe this

Guidance effectiveness can reverse with expertise [C003], making some adaptation necessary. But learner states are uncertain inferences [C007], making unnecessary complexity risky.

## Strongest counterarguments

Outcome-only tests may miss belonging, accessibility, agency, and preference. The comparison must therefore include a multidimensional value and harm model, not just test scores.

## What would change our mind

We would accept personalization without measurable learning gain where a clearly stated access, dignity, safety, or agency benefit outweighs cost and risk.

## Implications

Begin with rules a human can inspect. Introduce model-driven adaptation only with an explicit decision, evaluation plan, calibration checks, and fallback.

## Revision history

- 2026-08-31: adopted as a founding belief.

## P001 — Use progressive assistance

Type: principle  
Status: active  
Topics: scaffolding, learning-vs-performance, ai-tutoring  
Canonical path: `principles/P001-progressive-assistance.md`

# P001 — Use progressive assistance

## Principle

In deliberate learning, ask the learner to think, retrieve, predict, choose, or attempt before the system supplies the full solution. Escalate assistance based on evidence, and reveal the answer when further struggle is unlikely to be productive.

## Rationale

Unrestricted assistance can improve the current artifact while weakening later independent performance [C001]. Structured tutoring changes outcomes [C002], and the appropriate amount of guidance varies with expertise [C003].

## Apply when

The goal is capability development, the learner has enough prior knowledge to attempt, and errors are safe and recoverable.

## Do not apply blindly when

The user is explicitly in performance-support mode, the situation is urgent or safety critical, or the action creates construct-irrelevant accessibility barriers.

## Product patterns

- intent switch: learn, assess, or accomplish;
- attempt before reveal;
- progressive hints with learner-controlled escalation;
- self-explanation after a worked example;
- assistance-state logging.

## Falsifiers and measures

Compare against an answer-first condition using delayed independent performance, transfer, completion, frustration, and differential impact—not immediate task success alone.

## P002 — Use an evidence ledger for learner inferences

Type: principle  
Status: active  
Topics: learner-modelling, assessment-validity, ethics-and-governance  
Canonical path: `principles/P002-use-an-evidence-ledger.md`

# P002 — Use an evidence ledger for learner inferences

## Principle

Record the observation and the inference as different objects. Every consequential learner-state estimate should be answerable to: what happened, under which conditions, when, with what assistance, which model interpreted it, how certain is the estimate, and what may it be used for?

## Rationale

Learner models are probabilistic and construct-dependent [C007]. Trustworthy judgment requires a portfolio whose evidence remains interpretable [C008]. This infrastructure makes the learner model a compounding asset without converting it into unchallengeable surveillance [B003].

## Product patterns

- append-only observation events with correction records;
- versioned inferences and confidence;
- separate independent and AI-assisted evidence [B004];
- provenance links from recommendation back to observations;
- retention limits and user contestability;
- decision-specific permissions.

## Falsifiers and measures

Audit calibration, reversal after new evidence, explanation accuracy, user correction rates, privacy burden, and whether decisions improve against a simpler no-history baseline.

## P003 — Adapt and fade guidance with evidence

Type: principle  
Status: active  
Topics: scaffolding, learner-modelling, ai-tutoring  
Canonical path: `principles/P003-adapt-and-fade-guidance.md`

# P003 — Adapt and fade guidance with evidence

## Principle

Make scaffolding conditional on the target knowledge component, demonstrated performance, assistance history, confidence, and recentness. Fade one dimension at a time and verify independent success.

## Rationale

Guidance can reverse in value as expertise develops [C003], but the state used to adapt is uncertain [C007]. Personalization must therefore beat a transparent default rather than merely sound individualized [B005].

## Product patterns

- worked example → completion problem → independent problem;
- assistance budgets per capability;
- confidence-aware fallback when state evidence is weak;
- learner override and reason for adaptation;
- periodic unscaffolded probes.

## Falsifiers and measures

Evaluate independent learning, calibration, help misuse, frustration, fairness across groups, and the incremental effect over a well-designed fixed sequence.

## P004 — Retrieve and space important capabilities

Type: principle  
Status: active  
Topics: retrieval-and-spacing, transfer, product-measurement  
Canonical path: `principles/P004-retrieve-and-space.md`

# P004 — Retrieve and space important capabilities

## Principle

Create repeated, low-stakes opportunities for the learner to generate knowledge or action from memory, separated over time and varied enough to test the intended transfer.

## Rationale

Retrieval improves delayed retention and some transfer [C004], while distributed practice generally outperforms massing and should be tuned to the retention horizon [C005].

## Product patterns

- a revisit queue keyed to desired retention duration;
- prediction before explanation;
- retrieval with corrective feedback;
- mixed old and new practice;
- short independent probes after assisted work;
- graceful re-entry after missed sessions rather than punitive streaks.

## Falsifiers and measures

Measure delayed independent recall/application, near and far transfer, return rate, burden, and whether spacing rules help beyond a simple periodic default.

## P005 — Measure learning after assistance is removed

Type: principle  
Status: active  
Topics: learning-vs-performance, assessment-validity, product-measurement  
Canonical path: `principles/P005-measure-learning-after-assistance.md`

# P005 — Measure learning after assistance is removed

## Principle

Every learning claim should define support state, delay, and transfer distance. Evaluate independently after enough time to distinguish durable learning from temporary fluency.

## Rationale

Assisted success can coexist with impaired unaided performance [C001]. Retrieval and spacing effects demonstrate why immediate experience and later availability can point in different directions [C004, C005].

## Product patterns

- telemetry schemas that record assistance conditions;
- immediate, delayed, and transfer checkpoints;
- predeclared primary learning outcomes;
- dashboards that display performance and learning separately;
- no silent mastery credit for generated work.

## Falsifiers and measures

Validate whether cheaper assisted proxies predict the delayed independent outcome. Where they do, use them within their calibrated boundary rather than universalizing the result.

## P006 — Triangulate capability evidence

Type: principle  
Status: active  
Topics: assessment-validity, human-ai-collaboration, ethics-and-governance  
Canonical path: `principles/P006-triangulate-capability-evidence.md`

# P006 — Triangulate capability evidence

## Principle

Use an evidence portfolio proportional to the consequence of the decision. Vary task, time, context, and assistance where these variations matter to the construct; do not convert “more data” into “more truth.”

## Rationale

Learner-state estimates inherit assumptions and error [C007]. AI-era assessment guidance and validity theory support contextualized, programme-level evidence rather than confidence in a single produced artifact [C008].

## Product patterns

- construct maps and evidence requirements by decision;
- independent and supported demonstrations;
- conversation, artifact, process, and performance evidence with explicit roles;
- human review for consequential decisions;
- disagreement and missing-evidence states;
- minimal data collection consistent with the decision.

## Falsifiers and measures

Assess decision accuracy, fairness, consistency, construct coverage, burden, privacy impact, and the marginal value of each evidence channel.

## P007 — Preserve traceability from source to decision

Type: principle  
Status: active  
Topics: ethics-and-governance, product-measurement, institutional-design  
Canonical path: `principles/P007-preserve-research-traceability.md`

# P007 — Preserve traceability from source to decision

## Principle

Do not collapse sources, claims, beliefs, and design advice into an authoritative-sounding paragraph. Link them so a person or agent can inspect what supports a decision, where it might fail, and which part is normative judgment.

## Rationale

Inference without provenance becomes brittle authority [C007]. Multiple evidence channels help only when their meaning is preserved [C008]. An evidence-backed learner and product model compounds value through inspectability [B003].

## Product patterns

- stable IDs and typed relations;
- boundary conditions at retrieval time;
- decision records that cite principles and claims;
- source appraisal before claim promotion;
- explicit tensions and falsifiers;
- versioned changes rather than silent overwrites.

## Falsifiers and measures

Measure time to audit or correct a claim, rate of broken references, reviewer comprehension, decision reversibility, and retrieval usefulness to coding agents.

## Q001 — When does AI-assisted performance become durable learning?

Type: question  
Status: open  
Topics: learning-vs-performance, ai-tutoring, transfer, assessment-validity  
Canonical path: `questions/Q001-when-does-ai-performance-become-learning.md`

# Q001 — When does AI-assisted performance become durable learning?

## Why this matters

It is the highest-leverage question for a system that can either amplify capability or conceal its absence. It anchors review [R001].

## Scope and definitions

Compare supported performance with immediate independent, delayed retention, near transfer, and far transfer. Code learner expertise, subject, interaction policy, answer availability, feedback, teacher role, duration, stakes, and assessment alignment.

## What would answer it

A cumulative set of credible comparative studies, preferably with delayed unassisted outcomes, plus mechanism experiments that isolate pedagogical components.

## Next search

Update the structured search in `reviews/R001-learning-performance-gap/search-strategy.md`, prioritizing studies published after the current cutoff and backward/forward citation searching around [S001] and [S002].

## Q002 — What should a trustworthy learner model represent?

Type: question  
Status: open  
Topics: learner-modelling, assessment-validity, ethics-and-governance  
Canonical path: `questions/Q002-what-should-a-learner-model-represent.md`

# Q002 — What should a trustworthy learner model represent?

## Why this matters

The learner model is a candidate core asset for the Orqestra learning engine, but it can also become a scalable source of invalid inference and surveillance.

## Scope and definitions

Compare knowledge tracing, cognitive diagnosis, competency/evidence models, longitudinal portfolios, self-regulation and motivation models, and human-AI capability representations. Evaluate validity, calibration, contestability, usefulness, equity, privacy, and cost.

## What would answer it

An architectural synthesis plus product experiments comparing transparent baselines with increasingly complex models on actual intervention and decision quality.

## Next search

Begin with contemporary knowledge-tracing surveys, evidence-centred design, assessment validity, uncertainty communication, and learner-model ethics.

## Q003 — What is worth learning in an AI-rich world?

Type: question  
Status: open  
Topics: human-ai-collaboration, institutional-design, ethics-and-governance, motivation-and-agency  
Canonical path: `questions/Q003-what-is-worth-learning-in-an-ai-world.md`

# Q003 — What is worth learning in an AI-rich world?

## Why this matters

Optimizing learning is incoherent without a position on the capabilities worth developing. This is partly empirical and irreducibly normative.

## Scope and definitions

Consider foundational knowledge, judgment, verification, tool selection, problem framing, creativity, collaboration, self-regulation, civic agency, and the capacity to act without particular tools. Distinguish education’s economic, democratic, personal, and cultural purposes.

## What would answer it

No single study will. The atlas should triangulate philosophy of education, labour and technology evidence, disciplinary practice, learner voices, and democratic deliberation while keeping value judgments explicit.

## Next search

Create discourse notes spanning Papert, Biesta, critical edtech scholarship, capability approaches, and contemporary human-AI collaboration—steel-manning tensions rather than seeking a forced consensus.
